StudyLab / Docker lessons

Persistent storage, backup and safe shutdown

Find where the database files live and understand what happens when containers are replaced.

Open interactive lesson and complete code

What you are building

A student website, API and database running in containers

Package a .NET API and MVC website into images. Docker Compose starts them with SQL Server so the three services can work together.

SQL Server stores its files in a named Docker volume so they can survive container replacement.

Check the result

Follow the setup steps, start the Compose stack, open the website and add a student.

A container is disposable. Your students’ records should not be. A named volume keeps database files when the database container is recreated.

How to test this example in Visual Studio

Download the project below, extract it into its own folder, then open StudyLab.csproj. Wait for NuGet restore. Choose Build → Build Solution. For console projects choose Start Without Debugging. For API projects use View → Terminal, make sure the terminal is in the folder containing StudyLab.csproj, then run the command shown in the lesson. Do not paste all files into Program.cs: use the exact file names displayed below.

Prepare your computer

Install Docker Desktop with Linux containers enabled and the .NET10 SDK. For the full SQL Server stack use supported x64 hardware with enough memory for SQL Server. WPF does not run in the Linux ASP.NET image. Accept applicable vendor licences yourself during installation. Run docker version and docker compose version in a terminal; start Docker Desktop if the engine cannot be reached.

Prove persistence

docker compose down
docker compose up -d

Create a row before down. After up and readiness, read again. Expected: the row remains because school-data survives a normal down. The volume is not the same as a backup; losing/corrupting the volume can still lose data. Use SQL Server’s supported backup/restore process and practise recovery.

Destructive cleanup is a separate choice

docker compose down -v

This deletes the practice database volume and its rows. Use only when you intentionally want a fresh empty lab and have no needed data there. Do not teach students to run it as the normal stop command. Removing containers and deleting persistent data are different actions.

Development versus production

The example’s sa login and TrustServerCertificate are clearly labelled classroom shortcuts. A real stack needs a restricted application login, trusted certificates, reviewed migrations, backups, monitored storage and managed secrets. Do not scale a database by copying its writable files into several independent containers.

Try it yourself

Why did all rows disappear after down -v?

Worked answer

The -v flag deletes named volumes managed by this stack. Restore from a real backup if needed; recreating a volume does not recover old rows.

Is keeping a volume sufficient disaster recovery?

Worked answer

No. Back up and test restores to a different location/system.
